Issued at 245 AM EST Tue Nov 24 2026

Today-Tonight...Mid-level troughing across the central US will 
gradually begin strengthening today as it pushes eastward, with 
pulses of energy ahead of the trough drifting across the Florida 
peninsula. At the surface, a weakening boundary is forecast to 
stall across north Florida, with broad lows settling off the 
Georgia coast and along the Florida-Alabama border. This set-up 
will support slowly increasing moisture locally, resulting in 
building cloud coverage in the mid and upper levels. The passing 
energy aloft may provide just enough support for the development 
of light sprinkles across the area, especially through the morning
and early afternoon hours. Otherwise, a gloomy but mostly dry day
is in store for east central Florida with temperatures generally 
in the low to mid 70s. 

Tonight, an area of low pressure is forecast to develop across 
the southeastern Gulf near Cuba, with northeasterly flow locally 
helping to advect more moisture from the Atlantic towards the 
Florida peninsula. As a result, rain chances begin to increase 
tonight, with 20-40% PoPs near and north of the I-4 corridor and 
50-60% PoPs southward. At this time, storm chances remain 
primarily confined to the local Atlantic waters through the 
overnight period. WPC maintains portions of east central Florida 
in a Marginal Risk (1 out of 4) of excessive rainfall starting 
tonight, focused across the Treasure Coast counties, Brevard 
County, and Okeechobee County. A Flood Watch will begin at 1 AM 
across these areas tonight given the ongoing sensitivities from 
prior rainfall events. Overnight temperatures fall into the 60s.

Wednesday-Thursday...The aforementioned mid-level trough becomes 
further enhanced by a closed low shifting southward across the 
midwest, helping the trough dig into the southeastern US 
Wednesday into Thursday. By Thursday, the trough axis is 
anticipated to be positioned directly over the Florida peninsula,
lifting northeastward through the remainder of the day. This mid-
level support will help lift the surface low across south Florida,
passing near east central Florida. Rain chances will continue to 
increase through Wednesday as the low lifts northeastward, ranging
from 40-80% with the highest chances focused primarily across the
Treasure Coast. A Marginal Risk (1 out of 4) of excessive 
rainfall will remain in effect through Wednesday for the same 
areas mentioned earlier, and the Flood Watch remains in effect 
through 1 AM Thursday. Guidance and ensembles continue to favor 
rainfall totals around 1-2" in these areas, with areas farther 
north forecast to receive closer to 0.5-1". There is a 10% chance
of seeing totals across the south closer to 3-4", but confidence 
in this remains low at this time. Regardless of totals, however, 
any rainfall across fully saturated portions of east central 
Florida will likely result in additional or worsening flooding, 
with the greatest concern primarily focused across coastal 
communities and those along the St. Johns River. Embedded storms 
also cannot be ruled out with activity on Wednesday, though 
current guidance keeps chances around 20%. At this time, primary 
storm threats look to be lightning strikes and wind gusts up to 50
mph. It is important to note that if breaks in the clouds allow 
for daytime heating to occur, the risk for strong to severe storms
would increase, especially across areas south of Melbourne and 
Kissimmee. At this time, however, chances and confidence remain 
too low for strong to severe storm development. Trends will 
continue to be closely monitored.

Unlike recent heavy rainfall events, this low is anticipated to 
move quickly through the area rather than linger over a few days. 
By Thursday, the low is forecast to pull farther northeast and 
away from Florida, aided by the trough directly overhead. Some 
lingering shower activity cannot be ruled out through the morning 
and early afternoon hours given the trough axis aloft, so 
continued to maintain a 20-30% chance of showers on Thanksgiving 
Day. Conditions then trend drier through the remainder of Thursday
into the overnight hours. Strong offshore flow develops behind 
the low, with breezy winds at 10 to 15 mph and gusts up to 30 mph 
possible at times. Temperatures both Wednesday and Thursday will 
range from the upper 60s up north into the upper 70s down south 
each afternoon, with lows in the upper 50s to mid 60s Wednesday 
night cooling into the upper 40s to upper 50s Thursday night. 

High astronomical tides return midweek, with minor flooding 
anticipated along the east central Florida coast during the 
morning high tide cycles. A Coastal Flood Advisory is now in 
effect from 5 AM Wednesday through 11 AM Thursday. Additionally, 
building seas across the local Atlantic waters will lead to the
